Spectre affects all processors that use out of order execution. Meltdown impacts a couple of ARM chips and all of Intel's CPU's made in the last ten years, which seem to be the ones based on an Israeli design. No confirmation on the Israeli's doing this on purpose.

They are two exploits that attack two different vectors.

Meltdown affects Intel and some ARM processors and attacks a vulnerability in memory isolation between user and kernel access.

Spectre affects Intel, AMD, and ARM processors by attacking a vulnerability in speculative processes.

Meltdown only affects Intel processors and is a devastating bug with extremely severe consequences that can’t easily be fixed without re-writing lots of computer code and giving up some important efficiency shortcuts.

Spectre is a smaller, but still serious bug that affects a broader range of processors, including AMD.

The key difference here is scope. Spectre can expose certain small amounts of your computer’s memory to places that shouldn’t see them. Meltdown, by contrast, exposes (literally) more-than-all of your computer’s RAM. This makes it a more serious vulnerability by far.

TL;DR: AMD is the safest choice you can make today (2018-01-11). AMD Performance will not suffer due to patches

Remember there are actually 3 different exploits being talked about and most of the news on this conflates all three of them as the same thing, but they are NOT the same thing.

There is MeltDown (trivial to exploit, results in full READ access to anywhere in memory) and then there are 2 variants of Spectre: SPECTRE-1 and SPECTRE-2 make "probabilistic guesses" (based on delays in retrieval speed) on individual bits of memory. The attack then assembles these bits into bytes, so the leak speed is low.

MeltDown does not affect AMD at all. Full Stop. It affects all Intel CPUs since Pentium (I) and one variant of ARM cpe:2.3:h:arm:cortex-a:75:::::::* See NIST list of all MeltDown-affected CPUs

SPECTRE variant 1:

SPECTRE-1 can affect AMD, but it is extremely difficult to exploit. You need something in the Operating System providing JIT (just-in-time) compilation. This is already patched in Linux and Windows with no performance penalty.

Patched via the following:

1) a new instruction LFENCE added to the CPU via micro-code (bios or OS) update that allows the branch prediction buffers to be flushed prior to a context-switch (the active process changes)

2) OS update to call LFENCE prior to context switch

For this mitigation, there is no (or negligable) performance Impact.

SPECTRE variant 2:

AMD is not shown to be affected by SPECTRE-2. AMD is believed to not be vulnerable .

Mitigations for SPECTRE-2 (for ARM and Intel) include changes to how "near jumps" are called via a mechanism called a retpoline (like a trampoline but with 'ret' instructions to capture a rogue speculative execution pathway) or a microcode update (bios or os) that clears the branch prediction buffers. Branch prediction is one feature that makes modern CPUs fast, so clearing this on certain activities has an impact on performance.

Mitigations for SPECTRE-2 will cause performance loss

Side Note on Microsoft Patch The Windows patch for all variants of SPECTRE and MeltDown (even though the MeltDown portion of the Microsoft patch is not needed nor run on AMD systems) only blue-screened (did not "brick") 2 types of AMD CPUs that are both 10+ years old.

The problem was that Microsoft assumed that their patch-code would work without issue on these older CPUs, but did not verify their fix on an actual platform prior to release. The Microsoft "patch-flaw" has been corrected as of now.
